**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I.

The first time I realized words had weight was when my father told me he was leaving. Not in anger, not in tears—just a quiet sentence, delivered over a half-eaten plate of scrambled eggs. *"I can’t stay here anymore."* Seven words. They settled in my chest like stones.

I was twelve. Old enough to understand, young enough to believe that if I could just *find the right words*, I could change his mind. So I wrote him letters. Pages and pages, filled with memories (the time he taught me to ride a bike, how he laughed when I burned the pancakes), promises (*I’ll be better, I’ll listen more*), and desperate bargains (*If you stay, I’ll never ask for anything again*). I folded them into tiny squares and left them on his pillow, under his coffee mug, in the glove compartment of his car.

He left anyway.

That was the first lesson: words are not magic. They are tools, and like any tool, they can build or destroy, but they cannot bend the will of the universe.

---

II.

In college, I took a linguistics class where the professor claimed that language shapes reality. *"The Inuit have fifty words for snow,"* she said, *"because their survival depends on distinguishing between types of ice. We, in our climate-controlled bubbles, call it all ‘cold’ and move on."* She made it sound like a tragedy.

I raised my hand. *"So if I invent a word for the feeling of missing someone who’s still in the room, does that make it real?"*

She smiled. *"It makes it *communicable*."*

That night, I stayed up late, scribbling in a notebook:
- **Vellichor**: The sadness of unused books (I stole this one; it already existed).
- **Sonder**: The realization that every stranger has a life as complex as your own (also stolen).
- **Thalassophilia**: Love of the sea, but also the fear of what’s beneath it (mine, I think).

I never found the word for that hollow ache when someone you love is right beside you but already gone. Maybe it doesn’t exist because we’re not supposed to name it. Some weights are meant to be carried in silence.

---

III.

I worked in a call center for a summer. My job was to read from a script: *"We’re sorry for the inconvenience. Your refund will process in 7-10 business days."* The words were not mine. They belonged to the company, to the faceless algorithm that routed calls to my headset. I said them hundreds of times a day, my voice smooth as butter, while on the other end of the line, people screamed or cried or begged.

One woman, Mrs. Henderson, called every week for a month. Her husband had died, and the insurance company kept losing his claim. *"They keep asking for the same documents,"* she whispered. *"I don’t know what to do."*

I wasn’t supposed to deviate from the script. But that day, I did. *"Mrs. Henderson,"* I said, *"can you scan the documents and email them to me directly? I’ll walk them over to the processing team myself."*

She started sobbing. Not the angry, frustrated kind—the relieved kind, the kind that comes when someone finally *sees* you.

I got written up for breaking protocol. But that was the second lesson: sometimes, the right words are the ones you’re not supposed to say.

---

IV.

I fell in love with a poet once. He believed in the sacredness of language, in the way a single syllable could unravel a person. His poems were sparse, precise, like haikus carved from bone. He never said *"I love you."* Instead, he left notes in my apartment:
- *"Your laugh is the sound of a match striking."*
- *"I want to memorize the constellations of your freckles."*
- *"Stay."*

I thought it was romantic. Then I realized he was afraid of plain words, of the weight they carried. *"Love"* was too heavy. *"Stay"* was a plea he couldn’t voice aloud.

When he left, he didn’t write a poem. He sent a text: *"I’m sorry. I can’t."*

Three words. They gutted me.

---

V.

Now, I write for a living. Not poetry. Not letters. I write ad copy. *"Revolutionary!"* *"Life-changing!"* *"Limited time only!"* The words are light, hollow, designed to evaporate the moment the purchase is made. I am good at it. I know how to make people *want*.

Sometimes, at night, I open my laptop and type things I’ll never send:
- *"Do you ever think about the fact that we’re all just bags of water and electricity, hurtling through space on a rock?"*
- *"I still have the scar from where I fell off my bike when I was seven. Do you remember?"*
- *"I forgive you."*

I delete them all.

---

VI.

A thousand words. I’ve used 682 so far. What else is there to say?

Maybe this: Words are not the point. The point is the space between them. The pause before *"I do."* The silence after *"I’m sorry."* The way your name sounds when someone says it like a prayer.

Or maybe the point is that we keep trying anyway. We string together these clumsy symbols, these inadequate sounds, and hope that somehow, against all odds, they’ll be enough.

Here. Take these last 318 words. Fill them with whatever you need.

(Or leave them empty. That’s okay too.)
